arctic-small-tool-tradition.name: Arctic Small Tool tradition
arctic-small-tool-tradition.summary: A prehistoric culture that arose around Alaska and the Bering Strait about 2500 BC, marked by a microblade toolkit, whose people were the first to settle Arctic Canada and Greenland.

dorset-culture.name: Dorset culture
dorset-culture.summary: A Paleo-Eskimo culture in the North American Arctic, lasting from about 500 BCE until it died out by 1000–1500 CE, before the Thule (proto-Inuit) arrived. Inuit legends recall its people as the Tuniit.

qulliq.name: Qulliq
qulliq.summary: A traditional oil lamp used by circumpolar peoples including the Inuit, fueled by seal oil or blubber and made of soapstone; a vital source of Arctic warmth and light.

norton-tradition.name: Norton tradition
norton-tradition.summary: An archaeological culture along Alaska's Bering Strait coast from about 1000 BC to 800 AD, whose people hunted caribou and sea mammals and used new technologies like oil lamps and pottery.

banks-island.name: Banks Island
banks-island.summary: A large Arctic island in Canada's Northwest Territories, home to caribou and polar bears and once the summer range of most of the world's muskoxen.

ipiutak-site.name: Ipiutak site
ipiutak-site.summary: A large archaeological site at Point Hope, Alaska, with over 500 house remains and rich ivory carvings, representing the Ipiutak culture that existed from about 100 BCE to 800 CE.

point-hope-alaska.name: Point Hope, Alaska
point-hope-alaska.summary: A remote city on Alaska's northwestern coast with no road connections, and site of the ancient Ipiutak culture known for elaborate ivory carvings.

burin-lithic-flake.name: Burin
burin-lithic-flake.summary: Stone tool with a chisel-like edge used by prehistoric peoples for carving wood or bone and for engraving images.

st-lawrence-island.name: St. Lawrence Island
st-lawrence-island.summary: An island in the Bering Sea between Alaska and Russia, thought to be one of the last exposed remnants of the ancient land bridge joining Asia and North America.

otto-w-geist.name: Otto Geist
otto-w-geist.summary: Archaeologist, explorer and naturalist (1888–1963) who worked in the circumpolar north and for the University of Alaska for much of his life.

kinngait.name: Kinngait
kinngait.summary: An Inuit hamlet on Dorset Island near Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada, known as Cape Dorset until 2020.

ekven.name: Ekven
ekven.summary: An archaeological site in Chukotka, Russia, home to a 2,000-year-old Old Bering Sea culture cemetery of about 100 graves, including evidence of female shamans.

chukotka-autonomous-okrug.name: Chukotka
chukotka-autonomous-okrug.summary: The easternmost federal subject of Russia, bordering the Bering Strait opposite Alaska and home to ethnic Chukchi and other indigenous peoples.

pytheas.name: Pytheas
pytheas.summary: Greek geographer and explorer from Massalia (born c. 350 BC) who sailed to Northern Europe around 325 BC, circumnavigating Britain and becoming the first to describe the Arctic and the midnight sun.

massalia.name: Massalia
massalia.summary: An ancient Greek colony founded around 600 BCE on the Mediterranean coast, a major trading center whose ruins underlie modern Marseille, France's oldest city.

pillars-of-hercules.name: Pillars of Hercules
pillars-of-hercules.summary: The two promontories flanking the entrance to the Strait of Gibraltar, with the Rock of Gibraltar as the northern one; the term was already used in antiquity.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (384–322 BC) who founded the Peripatetic school, tutored Alexander the Great, and laid groundwork for modern science.

thule.name: Thule
thule.summary: A legendary, extremely remote northern land described by ancient Greek and Roman writers, later variously identified with places like Iceland, Greenland or Scandinavia.

strabo.name: Strabo
strabo.summary: Greek geographer (64/63 BC to about 24 AD) best known for his Geographica, a descriptive survey of the peoples and places known in his time.

geminus.name: Geminus of Rhodes
geminus.summary: A Greek astronomer and mathematician active in the 1st century BC, whose surviving work was an introductory astronomy textbook for students.

saqqaq-culture.name: Saqqaq culture
saqqaq-culture.summary: A Paleo-Inuit culture in southern Greenland, named after the settlement of Saqqaq, and the longest-residing culture in Greenland's history.

ptolemy.name: Ptolemy
ptolemy.summary: A Greco-Roman scholar of the 2nd century AD who wrote influential works on astronomy, geography and astrology; his geocentric model of the universe, promoted by the Catholic Church, was studied for over a thousand years.

servius-the-grammarian.name: Servius the Grammarian
servius-the-grammarian.summary: Roman grammarian of the late 4th and early 5th centuries, regarded as the most learned man of his generation in Italy, best known for his commentaries on Virgil.

chertov-ovrag.name: Chertov Ovrag
chertov-ovrag.summary: An archaeological site on Wrangel Island in the Russian Arctic, the westernmost known site of Paleo-Eskimo habitation, where stone and ivory tools including a toggle harpoon were found in 1975.

wrangel-island.name: Wrangel Island
wrangel-island.summary: An Arctic island of Russia's Chukotka region, about the size of Crete, lying between the Chukchi and East Siberian Seas and now a strictly protected nature reserve.

paleo-eskimo.name: Paleo-Eskimo
paleo-eskimo.summary: The peoples who inhabited the Arctic from Siberia to Greenland before the modern Inuit, with cultures developing from about 3900 BCE and the last, the Dorset, disappearing around 1500 CE.

independence-ii-culture.name: Independence II culture
independence-ii-culture.summary: A Paleo-Eskimo culture in northern and northeastern Greenland from about 700 to 80 BC, occupying much the same ground as the earlier Independence I culture.

independence-i-culture.name: Independence I culture
independence-i-culture.summary: A Paleo-Eskimo culture that lived in northern Greenland and the Canadian Arctic from about 2400 to 1900 BC, among the earliest known cultures in Greenland.

independence-fjord.name: Independence Fjord
independence-fjord.summary: A roughly 200 km long fjord in northern Greenland, after which two ancient Paleo-Eskimo cultures were later named.

peary-land.name: Peary Land
peary-land.summary: A peninsula in northern Greenland extending into the Arctic Ocean, reaching from Victoria Fjord to Independence Fjord and containing Cape Morris Jesup, Greenland's northernmost point.

thule-people.name: Thule people
thule-people.summary: The precursors of modern Inuit and Yupik peoples, who developed in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE, spread across the Arctic, and replaced the earlier Dorset culture by the 15th century.
